artiest/the-pied-pipers.text:
The Pied Pipers are an American pop vocal group, formed in the late 1930s. The first line-up had eight members drawn from three ensembles: Jo Stafford of The Stafford Sisters and seven male singers. They sang in the film Alexander's Ragtime Band in 1938. The arrangers Paul Weston and Axel Stordahl heard them and brought them to Tommy Dorsey's radio programme. Dorsey could not afford eight Pipers and asked for a quartet. It consisted of Jo Stafford, her husband at the time John Huddleston, Chuck Lowry and Billy Wilson, who was later replaced by Clark Yocum.

In 1940 Frank Sinatra joined Dorsey's orchestra. Together with the Pipers he made the big success I'll Never Smile Again. The group went on to have twelve hits with Dorsey, ten of them with Sinatra. Around Thanksgiving 1942 one of the Pipers was dismissed, whereupon the group left out of loyalty. Their last song with Dorsey, There Are Such Things, was at number one at the time.

In Los Angeles they signed with Capitol Records, where Paul Weston became arranger and bandleader. They also backed Johnny Mercer. Jo Stafford left in 1944 for a solo career, and June Hutton took her place. The Pipers had twelve hits at Capitol, including Dream, and appeared on Mercer's radio programme and with Sinatra. Their singing shows how in the 1940s a small vocal group could work both as accompaniment to a singer and as an act in its own right.
artiest/the-pied-pipers.listen: Listen to I'll Never Smile Again by Frank Sinatra and The Pied Pipers and notice how the group supports Sinatra's vocal. When do the voices of the Pipers come in?

artiest/the-plastic-ono-band.text:
The Plastic Ono Band was an English rock band and artists' collective, formed in 1968 and 1969 by John Lennon and Yoko Ono for their collaboration on music, sound art, films and conceptual projects. The idea of an open, plastic band came from Ono, as an exhibition idea in Berlin in 1967. For Lennon it was a way of separating his own work from that of The Beatles. They declared that the audience were themselves members of the band.

The group had a changing line-up that included Eric Clapton, Klaus Voormann, Alan White, Billy Preston, Jim Keltner, Keith Moon and Lennon's bandmates George Harrison and Ringo Starr. The first single under the name, Give Peace a Chance, was recorded in June 1969 during a bed-in in Montreal and released in July. It was the first single Lennon released outside The Beatles. Cold Turkey followed, with Starr on drums. In September 1969 the group played the Toronto Rock and Roll Revival festival.

Two albums appeared in 1970: John Lennon/Plastic Ono Band and Yoko Ono/Plastic Ono Band. After moving to New York in 1971, Lennon and Ono worked with Elephant's Memory, which led to Some Time in New York City (1972). From 2009 to 2015 Ono and her son Sean Lennon led a new version of the group. The Plastic Ono Band shows that pop music can also be an art project, in which a protest song and an experiment sit side by side.
artiest/the-plastic-ono-band.listen: Listen to Give Peace a Chance and notice the simple, repeated line in the chorus. Why can a large crowd of people sing along with a song like this?

artiest/the-plastic-people-of-the-univer.text:
The Plastic People of the Universe is a Czech rock band from Prague, regarded as the most important representative of the Prague underground culture between 1968 and 1989. In August 1968 the Prague Spring was ended by the invasion of the Warsaw Pact. Less than a month later the seventeen-year-old bassist Milan Hlavsa founded the band. It was strongly influenced by Frank Zappa and The Velvet Underground. The name comes from the song Plastic People on Absolutely Free by Zappa's Mothers of Invention. The art historian Ivan Jirous became manager and artistic director, in a role similar to that of Andy Warhol with the Velvet Underground.

In 1970 the communist regime withdrew the group's performing licence. Recording was not permitted, so fans circulated bootleg recordings of concerts. After the Canadian singer Paul Wilson left in 1972, the banned poet Egon Bondy wrote many of the lyrics. In 1974 they recorded their first studio album, Egon Bondy's Happy Hearts Club Banned, a nod to the Beatles' Sgt. Pepper, which was released in France in 1978. In 1976 band members and others from the underground were arrested and tried, and received prison sentences of eight to eighteen months. The trial became a turning point in the resistance to the regime and was one of the prompts for Václav Havel and others to write Charter 77.

After the Velvet Revolution in 1989 the group could play freely again. In 1997, at the suggestion of President Havel, it reunited for the twentieth anniversary of Charter 77, and in 1999 it performed at the White House with Lou Reed. In 2003 the Supreme Court overturned the verdicts of 1976. Hlavsa died in 2001.
artiest/the-plastic-people-of-the-univer.listen: Listen to a recording of Egon Bondy's Happy Hearts Club Banned by The Plastic People of the Universe. Notice the raw, experimental atmosphere and the lyrics sung or spoken in Czech, and remember that a record like this was a risk at the time.

artiest/the-police.text:
The Police was an English rock band, formed in London in 1977 by the American drummer Stewart Copeland. He wanted to take part in the new punk scene and brought in the singer and bassist Sting, whom he had seen in Newcastle in a jazz-rock band. After a brief period with the Corsican guitarist Henry Padovani, Andy Summers joined the band, an experienced guitarist who had played with Eric Burdon and the Animals, among others. From August 1977 The Police remained a trio. The bleached hair, later a trademark, came from a chewing-gum commercial.

The debut album Outlandos d'Amour (1978) contained Roxanne and Can't Stand Losing You. Reggatta de Blanc (1979) was the first of four consecutive albums to reach number 1 in Britain, with Message in a Bottle and Walking on the Moon. Zenyattà Mondatta (1980), recorded in three weeks in the Netherlands, followed, with Don't Stand So Close to Me, and then Ghost in the Machine (1981). The last album, Synchronicity (1983), topped the charts in Britain and America, among other countries, and Every Breath You Take became their only American number 1. At the height of their fame, in 1984, the band stopped. A reunion tour followed in 2007.

The Police used the outward trappings of punk, but the three musicians came from jazz and progressive rock and played in a much more refined way. They combined the energy of punk with the rhythms of reggae: a spacious guitar sound, Sting's springy bass and Copeland's nervous, precise drumming. In this way The Police became one of the first new wave bands with a large audience.
artiest/the-police.listen: Listen to Every Breath You Take and notice Andy Summers's guitar motif, which returns throughout the song in broken chords. Hear how bare everything else remains: a steady bass, quiet drums and Sting's voice.

artiest/the-prodigy.text:
The Prodigy is an English electronic band from Braintree, Essex. The producer and keyboard player Liam Howlett started the group in 1990 with the dancers Keith Flint and Leeroy Thornhill. Howlett DJed at the local club and made a mixtape for Flint, with his own tracks on the other side. On the cassette he scratched the word Prodigy, after his Moog Prodigy synthesizer. Flint and Thornhill devised dances to go with it, and so the band came into being. At the first gig MC Maxim also joined, coming from the reggae scene.

The band emerged from the underground rave scene. The debut Charly (1991) used little voices from a British public information film for children and became a big hit. Howlett did not want to be labelled children's rave afterwards. On Experience (1992) and above all on Music for the Jilted Generation (1994) the sound became harder and darker, with heavy breakbeats, techno and guitar samples. That last record was also a protest against a new law that restricted raves. Howlett himself called his style electronic punk.

In 1996 Firestarter was released, with Keith Flint as singer. With his punk haircut and screaming voice he brought rave to the rock audience. The album The Fat of the Land (1997), which also included Breathe, reached number 1 in sixteen countries, including America. The Prodigy are regarded as pioneers of big beat and breakbeat and are one of the most successful electronic groups ever. Thornhill left in 2000 and Flint died in 2019.
artiest/the-prodigy.listen: Listen to Firestarter from 1996. Notice the heavy breakbeat, the sharp, guitar-like sound and the snarling vocal of Keith Flint, which sounds more like punk than dance music.

artiest/the-quarrymen.text:
The Quarrymen was the skiffle group that John Lennon started in Liverpool in November 1956 with school friends from Quarry Bank High School, which gave the band its name. Skiffle was a craze in Britain at the time: it required neither expensive instruments nor great skill. Pete Shotton played washboard, another band member a tea-chest bass, and Lennon played guitar with banjo chords that his mother Julia had taught him. The repertoire came largely from Lonnie Donegan, supplemented with rock 'n' roll by Elvis Presley.

On 6 July 1957 the group played at a church fete in Woolton. There a friend introduced Lennon to Paul McCartney, who showed how he tuned his guitar and sang Twenty Flight Rock. Shortly afterwards McCartney became a member. At the beginning of 1958 he brought in his school friend George Harrison, although Lennon at first thought him too young. Skiffle gave way to rock 'n' roll, with Buddy Holly as an important example, and Lennon and McCartney began writing songs together. In July 1958 the group cut a record directly onto disc in a small studio in Liverpool, with That'll Be the Day by Buddy Holly and In Spite of All the Danger, a song by McCartney and Harrison.

Afterwards Lennon, McCartney and Harrison were left. They played under names such as Johnny and the Moondogs, and in 1960 they became The Beatles. The Quarrymen shows how the greatest pop group of the 1960s grew out of the do-it-yourself culture of skiffle.
artiest/the-quarrymen.listen: Listen to In Spite of All the Danger and notice how simple the recording is: everything was cut directly onto disc with a single microphone in the middle of the room. Hear how the boys' voices already blend together, as they later would in The Beatles.

artiest/the-ramblers.text:
The Ramblers was a Dutch jazz and dance orchestra, active from 1926 to 1964 and, with a different line-up, again from 1974 to 1998. The orchestra was founded on 1 September 1926 as a cabaret orchestra for the Amsterdam cabaret La Gaîté and, under the leadership of Theo Uden Masman, grew into the best-known dance orchestra in the Netherlands. It had the full instrumentation of a big band and played a mixture of jazz and light entertainment music.

In the 1930s and 1940s it was a popular radio orchestra and played an important part in spreading jazz in the Low Countries. The Christian broadcasters KRO and NCRV at first did not want this kind of music, but in 1933 the orchestra gave its first radio concert for the VARA, and from 1936 it was that broadcaster's regular house orchestra. More than two thousand radio concerts followed. The Ramblers brought swing to the Netherlands. Jack Bulterman was the driving force behind Dutch-language hit songs such as Wie is Loesje, Meneer de baron is niet thuis and Weet je nog wel die avond in de regen?, and in 1941 the orchestra made Dag Schatteboutje.

Because the orchestra had played for the Germans during the German occupation, Uden Masman was not allowed to lead his orchestra for a year after the war. The last performance of the original orchestra was on 11 April 1964. Jack Bulterman and Marcel Thielemans started The Ramblers again in 1974. In 1998 the band gave its last concert. Dag Schatteboutje was heard in the 2016 film Riphagen.
artiest/the-ramblers.listen: Listen to Dag Schatteboutje from 1941 and notice the swing and the Dutch vocals. Can you hear how a Dutch orchestra takes over the big-band sound from America?

artiest/the-revolution.text:
The Revolution was Prince's backing band. He formed the group in 1979 in Minneapolis, shortly after his first album, and wanted a mixed band of men and women from the start, following the example of Sly Stone. The line-up changed in the early years: Gayle Chapman made way for Lisa Coleman, André Cymone for Brown Mark, and Dez Dickerson for Wendy Melvoin. Together with Bobby Z. and Matt Fink they formed the core of the band. On the sleeve of 1999 from 1982 the band name is already printed in mirror image.

The big success came with Purple Rain in 1984, the first album officially credited to Prince and the Revolution. It topped the Billboard 200 and yielded the singles Let's Go Crazy and When Doves Cry, which both reached number one in the United States. Around the World in a Day followed in 1985, also a number one, and Parade in 1986, the soundtrack to the film Under the Cherry Moon. Kiss became the band's third number one.

The sound of The Revolution blended rock, funk, R&B, new wave, synth-pop and psychedelia. Wendy and Lisa in particular brought more pop and classical influences into Prince's music, and during the Parade tour the band gained a horn section for the jazzy arrangements. In this way the group belongs to the Minneapolis sound. After the last show in Yokohama in 1986 Prince disbanded the band, and part of the recordings for the unfinished album Dream Factory moved to Sign o' the Times. After his death in 2016 The Revolution got together again to play his music live.
artiest/the-revolution.listen: Listen to When Doves Cry and notice what is missing: a bass line. Hear how drum machine, keyboards and guitar nevertheless make a full, danceable record.

artiest/the-rh-factor.text:
The RH Factor was the group with which the American trumpeter Roy Hargrove linked jazz with funk, soul and hip hop in the early 2000s. The name refers to his own initials. Hargrove came from jazz and had already proved himself as one of the best-known trumpeters of his generation, but with this band he moved in a more urban and danceable direction.

The group released three albums: Hard Groove in 2003, Strength in 2004 and Distractions in 2006, which appeared on Verve Records. On Distractions Hargrove plays trumpet and flugelhorn and also sings himself. The band was made up of a flexible team of musicians, including Renée Neufville on vocals and keyboards, the saxophonist David Fathead Newman and keyboard players who played Wurlitzer, Rhodes, Moog and Clavinet. The soul singer D'Angelo sings on one of the tracks.

Critical opinion was divided. Some reviewers found Distractions a deeply satisfying, relaxed album with an urban soul feel; others found it crossover that was neither really jazz nor really funk. It is precisely that tension that makes the band interesting: The RH Factor shows how jazz musicians at the beginning of this century searched for a new connection with the soul and the groove of their own time.
artiest/the-rh-factor.listen: Listen to the opening section of a track from Distractions and notice the role of the trumpet alongside the electric keyboards: do you hear more jazz or more groove?

artiest/the-righteous-brothers.text:
The Righteous Brothers were an American duo of Bill Medley and Bobby Hatfield. Both came from Southern California and at first played in separate groups, until in 1962 they ended up together in a new version of the Paramours. A year later they carried on as a duo. They are said to owe their name to Black marines from the El Toro base, who shouted after a performance that it was righteous, brothers. The contrast between their voices defined their sound: Medley sang the low parts with his bass-baritone, Hatfield the high ones with his tenor.

The turning point came in 1964, when Phil Spector signed them to his label Philles. Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil wrote You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin' for them, a number one in 1965 and a high point of Spector's Wall of Sound. Just Once in My Life, Unchained Melody and Ebb Tide followed. After the move to Verve in 1966 they reached the top again with (You're My) Soul and Inspiration. In 1968 the two split up, and in 1974 they returned with Rock and Roll Heaven. In 1990 Unchained Melody got a second life through the film Ghost.

The term blue-eyed soul was first attached to their music, in 1964, by Black disc jockeys. Later it became the name for all white singers who made music that was then regarded as Black. In 2003 the two were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, shortly before Hatfield's death. Medley continued in 2016 with Bucky Heard.
artiest/the-righteous-brothers.listen: Listen to You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin' and follow how Medley starts low and Hatfield comes in high later. Notice how the accompaniment grows along with them into an enormous, full sound.

artiest/the-rolling-stones.text:
The Rolling Stones were formed in London in 1962. The singer Mick Jagger and the guitarist Keith Richards already knew each other from Dartford, and the guitarist Brian Jones chose the name, after a record by the bluesman Muddy Waters. By early 1963 the bassist Bill Wyman and the drummer Charlie Watts had joined. Together with The Beatles, the Stones were at the forefront of the British Invasion: British bands that brought American rhythm and blues back to America.

Manager Andrew Loog Oldham pushed Jagger and Richards to write songs themselves. (I Can't Get No) Satisfaction (1965) became their first number 1 hit in America; Richards plays the riff through a Maestro Fuzz-Tone, one of the first effects pedals. In Paint It, Black (1966) Jones plays sitar. After an excursion into psychedelia with Their Satanic Majesties Request (1967), the band returned to blues and rhythm and blues on Beggars Banquet (1968). Jones left the group in June 1969 and drowned a month later; Mick Taylor took his place. Let It Bleed (1969), Sticky Fingers (1971) and Exile on Main St. (1972) followed. At the end of 1974 Taylor left, and Ronnie Wood replaced him.

The Stones kept moving with the times: Miss You (1978) is rock with a disco bass line. The acoustic Wild Horses reveals the influence of the country singer Gram Parsons, and in this way the Stones also belong to the history of country rock. Watts died in 2021. In 2023 Hackney Diamonds appeared, their first album of new original material in eighteen years.
artiest/the-rolling-stones.listen: In Paint It, Black Brian Jones plays the melody on a sitar, and Bill Wyman looks for a heavier bass part with the bass pedals of a Hammond organ. Listen to how the sitar sets out the Eastern-sounding melody in the intro, and how beneath it the low notes of those organ pedals rumble along.

artiest/the-ronettes.text:
The Ronettes was a girl group from Washington Heights in New York, with the singer Veronica (Ronnie) Bennett, her older sister Estelle and their cousin Nedra Talley. They sang together as children at their grandmother's home and, as teenagers, performed at an amateur night at the Apollo Theater. As Ronnie and the Relatives they recorded a few singles for Colpix from 1961, without success. In the meantime they danced the twist at the Peppermint Lounge and sang backing vocals in the shows of the radio presenter Murray the K. That was where their striking look arose: heavy eye make-up and high-piled hair.

In 1963 they auditioned for the producer Phil Spector. He really wanted only Ronnie, but her mother insisted that he take the whole group. In July 1963 they recorded Be My Baby, written by Spector, Jeff Barry and Ellie Greenwich. The song reached number two in America and became their best-known record. Baby, I Love You, (The Best Part of) Breakin' Up and Walking in the Rain followed, and in 1964 their only album, Presenting the Fabulous Ronettes Featuring Veronica. In England The Rolling Stones were their opening act, and in 1966 they toured with The Beatles. In 1967 the group split up.

Be My Baby is a textbook example of Spector's Wall of Sound: a large group of musicians and backing singers, among them the young Cher, who together sound like an enormous wall of sound, with Ronnie's voice rising above it. Brian Wilson of The Beach Boys was so impressed that he wrote Don't Worry Baby as a tribute to the group.
artiest/the-ronettes.listen: Listen to Be My Baby and notice the drums that open the song: a bare, instantly recognisable rhythm. Then hear how the wall of sound builds up, with strings, percussion and a choir, and how Ronnie's voice keeps rising above it.

artiest/the-roots.text:
The Roots come from Philadelphia. The rapper Tariq Black Thought Trotter and the drummer Ahmir Questlove Thompson met at the city's school for the arts and at first played on the street, with Questlove on buckets and Black Thought rapping over him. After a series of name changes it became The Roots. Because things were not working out at home, the group spent some time in London, where the self-released debut Organix appeared in 1993. The band then signed with DGC/Geffen and Do You Want More?!!!??! was released, which is regarded today as a classic of jazz rap.

The group is known for a jazzy, versatile approach to hip hop with real instruments: drums, bass, keyboards and later also guitar and sousaphone. Black Thought himself called it organic hip hop jazz. Illadelph Halflife in 1996 brought the first top 40 entry on the Billboard 200 and many guests, including Common, D'Angelo and Q-Tip. That collaboration laid the foundation for the Soulquarians and for the band's link with neo-soul. Things Fall Apart in 1999 was the big breakthrough album, with You Got Me with Erykah Badu and Eve and Jill Scott, which won a Grammy. Later came Phrenology, The Tipping Point, Game Theory, How I Got Over and undun, a concept album about the semi-fictional Redford Stephens, among others.

The Roots are also the regular house band of The Tonight Show with Jimmy Fallon, having previously been the house band of Late Night. They backed Jay-Z on MTV Unplugged and made albums with John Legend, Betty Wright and Elvis Costello. They are often called the first real band of hip hop.
artiest/the-roots.listen: Listen to You Got Me from Things Fall Apart and follow how rap, vocals and live accompaniment alternate. Notice how Questlove's drums carry the song without making it heavy.

artiest/the-runaways.text:
The Runaways was an American rock band that existed from 1975 to 1979. The producer Kim Fowley wanted to put together an all-girl band, at a time when, according to Joan Jett, almost no young girls played guitar. He found Jett and the drummer Sandy West in Los Angeles, and later Lita Ford, the singer Cherie Currie and the bassist Jackie Fox joined. The line-up was settled in 1975, in 1976 the group signed with Mercury and the debut The Runaways was released. A year later came Queens of Noise and Waitin' for the Night, followed by And Now... The Runaways.

Their best-known songs are Cherry Bomb, Hollywood, Queens of Noise and a cover of Rock & Roll by The Velvet Underground. The music sat somewhere between hard rock, glam rock and punk, with loud guitars and raw vocals. In the United States the band never really became big, but in Japan the group broke through thanks to Cherry Bomb. According to Jett, their arrival there resembled Beatlemania, and the album Live in Japan went gold. In the meantime the band hung out with the Ramones and the British punk groups.

Tensions grew within the band. Jett wanted to move towards punk and glam rock, Ford and West stuck to hard rock and heavy metal, and in 1979 the band fell apart. The influence remained great. Joan Jett started her own label Blackheart Records and later scored with I Love Rock 'n' Roll. Lita Ford had solo success, and Micki Steele, the first bassist, went to The Bangles. The group showed that girls could carry a rock band themselves.
artiest/the-runaways.listen: Listen to Cherry Bomb and notice Cherie Currie's raw vocal and the sharp guitars. Do you hear more punk or more hard rock?

artiest/the-scene.text:
The Scene is a Dutch rock band from Amsterdam built around the singer, guitarist, composer and producer Thé Lau. Lau played in groups such as Music Garden and the Neerlands Hoop Express in the 1970s and founded The Scene in 1979. The line-up changed almost monthly at first, but the sound remained recognisable thanks to Lau's raw, husky voice. In 1980 the music magazine OOR declared The Scene the best Dutch band without a record. The debut album The Scene was almost entirely in English and received good reviews, but sold little.

For years the band released records on its own. The breakthrough came with Rij rij rij (1988), produced by Rick de Leeuw of the Tröckener Kecks. After a contract with Phonogram, the fully Dutch-language album Blauw appeared in 1990, with the singles Rigoreus and Iedereen is van de wereld. The title song became a hit first in Flanders and then in the Netherlands too, and the band played at Torhout-Werchter. Open (1992) was received as a masterpiece, and in early 1993 The Scene received the Popprijs, the Dutch pop award. That same year Iedereen is van de wereld appeared again, on a joint single with De Dijk, for Doctors Without Borders. Avenue de la Scene (1993) and Arena (1996) followed, among others.

The Scene made robust guitar rock with soul influences. OOR called Open a passionate soul record with compelling rock, and the Popprijs jury praised the poetic Dutch-language lyrics in sober arrangements. The band was active until 2014 and announced a return in 2025, with Syb van der Ploeg as singer.
artiest/the-scene.listen: Listen to Iedereen is van de wereld and notice Thé Lau's voice: raw and husky, but also tender. Hear how the band keeps its playing sober, so that the lyrics get all the room.

artiest/the-selecter.text:
The Selecter is an English ska band from Coventry, formed in 1979. It began with an instrumental track that the guitarist Neol Davies, the drummer John Bradbury and the trombonist Barry Jones had already recorded in 1977. When The Specials needed a B-side for their debut single Gangsters in 1979, that track was put on it under the name The Selecter. It became the first single on the 2 Tone label. After the success Davies quickly put together a real band, with musicians from Coventry's reggae scene, the singer Arthur Gaps Hendrickson and the singer Pauline Black.

In October 1979 On My Radio was released, written by Davies, and the band toured England with Madness and The Specials. Three Minute Hero, Missing Words and, in February 1980, the debut album Too Much Pressure followed. Later that year the group left 2 Tone. The second album, Celebrate the Bullet (1981), was darker and slower, with influences from new wave. Soon afterwards Black left, and the band fell apart. From 1991 The Selecter returned in changing line-ups, in recent years under Black's leadership.

The Selecter belonged to the core of the 2 Tone movement, which mixed ska with the energy of punk. The band was one of the few 2 Tone groups with both Black and white members and with both men and women. Pauline Black, in a man's suit and a trilby, sang about racism and sexism. In this way she became a role model for later ska artists such as Gwen Stefani of No Doubt.
artiest/the-selecter.listen: Listen to On My Radio and notice the ska rhythm: the guitar and the organ keep playing on the offbeat, between the beats. Hear how Pauline Black sings over it, fast and sharp, with the energy of punk.

artiest/the-shadows.text:
The Shadows was an English instrumental rock group, formed in 1958 under the name The Drifters. They began as the backing band of the singer Harry Webb, who started calling himself Cliff Richard. Their first single with him was Move It. In 1959 the guitarist Hank Marvin, rhythm guitarist Bruce Welch, bassist Jet Harris and drummer Tony Meehan joined the group. Marvin caught the eye of the producer Johnny Foster in a Soho coffee bar, with his guitar playing and his Buddy Holly-style glasses. Because an American vocal group had the same name and threatened legal action, Harris came up with the new name in July 1959.

In 1960 their instrumental single Apache reached number one in the United Kingdom. Other number ones were Kon-Tiki, Wonderful Land, Foot Tapper and Dance On! In 1961 Brian Bennett replaced Meehan, and Harris left in 1962. They remained Richard's backing band until 1968 and then split up, but got together again in the 1970s. Until 2007 they were the fifth most successful act in the British singles chart, after Elvis Presley, the Beatles, Cliff Richard and Madonna.

The Shadows played in the line-up of lead guitar, rhythm guitar, bass and drums, and built their sound on Fender guitars and Vox amplifiers. They were the first backing band that also had commercial success of its own. In this way they set an example to many British boys: a group could manage on its own, with guitars. For the beat groups of the 1960s, the Beatles themselves among them, that was an important cradle.
artiest/the-shadows.listen: Listen to Apache by The Shadows. Notice how the lead guitar's melody takes the place of a singer, with the echo and the driving rhythm of the rest of the band beneath it.

artiest/the-shirelles.text:
The Shirelles were an American girl group, formed in 1957 by four classmates from high school in Passaic, New Jersey: Shirley Owens, Doris Coley, Addie 'Micki' Harris and Beverly Lee. They were discovered by Florence Greenberg, who started a label of her own for them, first Tiara and later Scepter. With Will You Love Me Tomorrow they scored the first number 1 by a Black girl group on the Billboard Hot 100, and in doing so they opened the way for the girl groups of the 1960s.

The group worked with the producer and writer Luther Dixon. After Tonight's the Night (1960), Will You Love Me Tomorrow followed in November 1960, written by the husband-and-wife team Gerry Goffin and Carole King from the song factory around the Brill Building. Shirley Owens at first found the song too country, until a string arrangement was added. The recording was made at Bell Sound in New York, with session musicians such as the pianist Paul Griffin and the drummer Gary Chester. In early 1961 the single reached number 1 in the United States; in England it reached number 4. Dedicated to the One I Love and Soldier Boy, which became number 1 again in 1962, followed among others.

The Beatles were fans and recorded Baby It's You and Boys for their debut album Please Please Me (1963). Carole King sang Will You Love Me Tomorrow herself in 1971, more slowly, on her album Tapestry. In 1996 The Shirelles were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. They were followed by girl groups such as The Crystals, The Ronettes and The Supremes.
artiest/the-shirelles.listen: In Will You Love Me Tomorrow, listen to the contrast between the voice and the accompaniment: Shirley Owens sings the question in the lyrics softly and uncertainly, while the strings and the rolling rhythm beneath build up a small drama. Notice too the soft backing vocals of the other three, which surround her voice like a cushion.

artiest/the-slits.text:
The Slits were a British band from London, one of the first all-female groups of punk and later post-punk. They formed in October 1976, after the fourteen-year-old Ari Up was asked to start a band following a Patti Smith concert at the Hammersmith Odeon. Together with Palmolive, Viv Albertine and Tessa Pollitt she formed the first line-up. In 1977 the group toured with The Clash, and part of those performances can be seen in The Punk Rock Movie.

The sound changed when the drummer Palmolive left in 1978 and Budgie succeeded her. The raw, drum-dominated sound of the Peel Sessions was built more on the bass and took a lot from reggae, dub and world music. That was how the debut album Cut sounded, produced by Dennis Bovell and released in September 1979 on Island Records. Neneh Cherry sang along as an extra vocalist. The sleeve showed the band members covered in mud and wearing loincloths, and became almost as famous as the music. After that the band became more experimental, collaborated with The Pop Group and released Return of the Giant Slits in 1981, before stopping in 1982.

In 2005 the group returned with Ari Up and Tessa Pollitt and new members. Trapped Animal appeared in 2009. After the death of Ari Up in 2010 the band stopped. Cut is regarded as one of the defining records of post-punk, and the group showed how punk could open up to dub and rhythm.
artiest/the-slits.listen: Listen to Typical Girls and notice the rhythmic foundation and Ari Up's playful, sometimes skewed vocals. Hear how the band lets punk and reggae run into each other.

artiest/the-smashing-pumpkins.text:
The Smashing Pumpkins is an American alternative rock band from Chicago, formed in 1988 by the singer and guitarist Billy Corgan, the guitarist James Iha, the bassist D'arcy Wretzky and the drummer Jimmy Chamberlin. After the end of his goth and metal band The Marked, Corgan returned to his home city and worked in a record shop, where he met Iha. Together they first wrote songs with a drum machine, strongly influenced by The Cure and New Order. Only when a club demanded a real drummer did Chamberlin join, a jazz drummer.

The debut album Gish appeared in 1991 and was a success in the underground. Siamese Dream from 1993 brought the group popularity, despite a difficult recording process. Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness from 1995 went to the top of the American album chart. Adore followed in 1998 and Machina and Machina II in 2000. Quarrels, drug use and falling sales then led to a split. In 2006 Corgan and Chamberlin got together again for Zeitgeist, and later came Oceania in 2012 and Cyr in 2020, among others. Corgan is the only constant in the line-up.

The group's music sounds dense and layered and takes in influences from goth, metal, grunge, psychedelia, progressive rock, shoegaze and electronics. It sold thirty million albums and helped alternative rock break through to a large audience. In Today, from Siamese Dream, they show how far apart music and lyrics can be: a cheerful-sounding motif beneath a dark lyric.
artiest/the-smashing-pumpkins.listen: Listen to Today by The Smashing Pumpkins. Notice the cheerful guitar motif at the start and compare it with what the lyrics say.

artiest/the-smiths.text:
The Smiths was an English band from Manchester, started in 1982 by the guitarist Johnny Marr and the singer Morrissey. Marr knocked on Morrissey's door, following the example of the songwriters Leiber and Stoller, because he had heard that Morrissey wrote good lyrics. They shared a love of poetry, literature and the New York Dolls. The bassist Andy Rourke and the drummer Mike Joyce completed the group. Morrissey chose the name because it was the most ordinary name he could think of: time for ordinary people to show themselves.

In 1983 the band signed with the independent label Rough Trade. After Hand in Glove, This Charming Man became the first hit, partly thanks to the support of John Peel on BBC Radio 1. The debut album The Smiths (1984) reached number two in England. Meat Is Murder (1985) was more political and reached number 1. The Queen Is Dead (1986) appears on many lists of the best albums of all time. The single Panic also appeared in 1986. After Strangeways, Here We Come (1987) the band split up, mainly because of tensions between Morrissey and Marr.

In an age of synthesizers and new romantics, The Smiths chose guitar, bass and drums. Marr's clear, melodic guitar playing stood against Morrissey's baritone and his literary, sarcastic lyrics about loneliness, unrequited love and resistance to authority. With plain clothes and sleeves featuring photos of old film stars they built an image of their own. The Smiths are regarded as forerunners of indie rock and were a great influence on Britpop.
artiest/the-smiths.listen: Listen to Panic and notice the lyrics: Morrissey calls for the DJ to be hanged, because the radio says nothing about his life. Hear how that criticism sounds over a stomping glam rock rhythm, borrowed from Metal Guru by T. Rex.

artiest/the-sonics.text:
The Sonics are an American garage rock band from Tacoma, Washington, started in 1960 by the teenage guitarist Larry Parypa. At first it was an instrumental group, with his brother Andy on bass. The well-known line-up took shape when Gerry Roslie joined on keyboards, together with the drummer Bob Bennett and the saxophonist Rob Lind. They really got going in 1964, when Roslie took over the vocals. They played at local venues such as the Red Carpet and Olympia's Skateland.

The group played rock standards such as Louie Louie and Skinny Minnie, but also original songs such as Strychnine, Psycho and The Witch. Their albums included Here Are The Sonics!!! from 1965, Merry Christmas in the same year, Boom from 1966 and Introducing the Sonics from 1967. This Is the Sonics followed in 2015.

The Sonics' music is hard, raw and fast. The songs revolve around simple chords played with a speed and a tonal aggression that were new at the time. As a result they became an important influence on later punk bands, such as the Stooges and the Cramps. The White Stripes, Nirvana and The Hives have also cited them as an inspiration. In the course they stand at the roots of garage rock.
artiest/the-sonics.listen: Listen to Psycho and notice the screaming vocals and the heavy, distorted guitars. Can you hear how little the song needs: a few chords and a lot of energy?

artiest/the-soul-stirrers.text:
The Soul Stirrers are an American gospel group with a career of more than a hundred years. Roy Crain started his first jubilee-style quartet in 1926 in Trinity, Texas. In the early 1930s, in Houston, he joined an existing group, on condition that it took the name Soul Stirrers. The singer R.H. Harris, also from Trinity, soon became the musical leader.

Harris changed the way quartets sang. He used falsetto, a style with roots in African music that was new to the jubilee singing of the time. He also devised the swing lead, in which two singers shared the lead, so that the intensity could rise without losing the four-part harmony. As a result the quartet had five members. The group improvised lyrics, sang in slowed-down fashion and repeated words in the background as rhythmic and emotional support. They widened the repertoire from spirituals to newer gospel songs and gave the individual singers more room.

At Specialty Records they recorded songs such as By and By and In That Awful Hour. After Harris left in 1950, the nineteen-year-old Sam Cooke became lead singer. With him came Jesus Gave Me Water, a big hit that brought the group fame. When Cooke chose a pop career in 1957, the group's heyday was over. His move shows how gospel pointed the way to soul, R&B and doo-wop. In 1989 the group was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as one of the early influences.
artiest/the-soul-stirrers.listen: Listen to Jesus Gave Me Water and notice how the lead singer is caught by repeating backing voices. Can you hear how the lead builds an emotional tension above the harmony?

artiest/the-soulquarians.text:
The Soulquarians were a shifting collective of experimental Black musicians, active in the late 1990s and early 2000s. They began with the singer and multi-instrumentalist D'Angelo, the drummer and producer Questlove of The Roots and the producer and rapper J Dilla, with the keyboard player James Poyser as the fourth. The name comes from the star sign Aquarius, the shared birth sign of the founders. Later, Erykah Badu, Roy Hargrove, Bilal, the bassist Pino Palladino, Q-Tip, Mos Def, Talib Kweli and Common, among others, joined.

The centre of the collective was Electric Lady Studios in New York, Jimi Hendrix's studio, with a lot of old equipment. The sessions began in 1997, when D'Angelo and Questlove were preparing his album Voodoo. They produced, among others, Things Fall Apart by The Roots in 1999, Mama's Gun by Badu and Like Water for Chocolate by Common, both in 2000, and later Phrenology by The Roots. Musicians played on each other's records. The style is described as neo-soul, alternative hip hop, progressive soul and jazz fusion, with offbeat rhythms, strange chords and a warm, organic sound. The lyrics dealt with personal themes and social concerns rather than with stock hip hop clichés.

The collective came to an end when some experimental records disappointed commercially, among them Electric Circus by Common and Love for Sale by Bilal, which stayed on the shelf for years. Questlove also named an article in Vibe as the beginning of the end. J Dilla died in 2006. The influence, however, remained great and can be heard in the generation of Robert Glasper, Esperanza Spalding and Kendrick Lamar.
artiest/the-soulquarians.listen: Listen to You Got Me by The Roots and notice how live drums, Rhodes and vocals give each other room. Can you hear how warm and loose the sound is?

artiest/the-special-aka.text:
The Special AKA is the name under which the English group The Specials released part of its work. The band was formed in Coventry in 1977 by the songwriter and keyboard player Jerry Dammers, together with the guitarist Lynval Golding and the bassist Horace Panter, among others. Terry Hall soon joined as singer, and Roddy Radiation as guitarist in 1978. The group was first called the Automatics and then the Special A.K.A., a name that was shortened to The Specials. Joe Strummer of The Clash invited them as the opening act on the On Parole tour, and Neville Staple, at first a roadie, became a full member after that tour.

Their music combined the danceable rhythms of ska and rocksteady with the energy of punk, and carried a social and political message. The band members wore 1960s fashion, such as pork pie hats and mohair suits. In 1979 Dammers founded the label 2 Tone, on which their debut single Gangsters appeared. In 1980 the EP The Special A.K.A. Live!, with Too Much Too Young, reached number one in the United Kingdom, and in 1981 the recession single Ghost Town did the same. Hall, Staple and Golding then left to form Fun Boy Three.

The remaining members carried on as The Special AKA. In 1984 the single Free Nelson Mandela was released, which reached the British top ten. Dammers then disbanded the group. In 1993 the band got together again without him, until Terry Hall died in December 2022. Anti-racism was a core of the group for Dammers: he wanted to bring Black and white musicians together, and the group showed that a danceable song can also carry a political protest.
artiest/the-special-aka.listen: Listen to Free Nelson Mandela by The Special AKA. Notice the cheerful, danceable rhythm and the way the lyrics make a clear political demand.

artiest/the-specials.text:
The Specials came from Coventry, an industrial city in the English Midlands. The band began in 1977, first as The Automatics and then as The Coventry Automatics. The keyboard player Jerry Dammers was the driving force. He founded the label 2 Tone in 1979, and The Specials became the figureheads of the movement named after that label. The line-up was deliberately mixed, with Black and white musicians, at a time when the far right was looking for new members among unemployed young people.

The band played ska from Jamaica, but faster and with the energy of punk. In 1979 the first single, Gangsters, and the debut album The Specials, produced by Elvis Costello, were released. The vocals were shared between Terry Hall and Neville Staple, and horn players such as the trombonist Rico Rodriguez gave the sound its Jamaican colour. In 1980 the EP Too Much Too Young was at number 1 in England. Ghost Town was released in June 1981 and spent three weeks at number 1, in a summer of riots in English cities. It was the last single by the original line-up.

Immediately afterwards Hall, Staple and the guitarist Lynval Golding left to start Fun Boy Three. Dammers continued as The Special AKA and had a hit in 1984 with Free Nelson Mandela. Without him the band returned to the stage in 2009, and the album Encore reached number 1 in the British album chart in 2019. Terry Hall died in 2022. The influence reached the Netherlands too: Doe Maar took over the ska of 2 Tone and sang it in Dutch.
artiest/the-specials.listen: In Ghost Town the song fades in and out again in a ghostly sound: producer John Collins made that with a synthesizer. Notice too Jerry Dammers's Hammond organ, which slides over diminished chords, and the flute and the trombone playing the Eastern-sounding line.

artiest/the-stanley-brothers.text:
The Stanley Brothers were an American bluegrass duo of the brothers Carter Stanley and Ralph Stanley. They were born on a small farm in Dickenson County, Virginia, and as children listened on the radio to the Monroe Brothers, J.E. Mainer's Mountaineers and the Grand Ole Opry. They began as the Lazy Ramblers and performed on radio station WJHL in Johnson City, Tennessee. After the Second World War they formed the Clinch Mountain Boys in November 1946, the first band to follow Bill Monroe's sound.

Carter played guitar and sang lead, Ralph played banjo and sang a strong, high tenor. From December 1946 they played on radio station WCYB in Bristol, Tennessee, and in 1947 they made their first recordings for Rich-R-Tone Records. In 1948 Ralph switched to Earl Scruggs's three-finger banjo style. From 1949 they recorded for Columbia Records. Albums such as Hymns and Sacred Songs and Mountain Song Favorites appeared in 1959. After Carter's death in 1966 Ralph carried on under the name The Clinch Mountain Boys, until his own death in 2016.

The Stanley Brothers played bluegrass with a strong mountain spirit, with high harmony singing and sharp banjo playing. They gave the music of Appalachia a sound of its own. In 2026 they were inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame.
artiest/the-stanley-brothers.listen: Listen to I'm a Man of Constant Sorrow and notice Ralph's high singing. Can you hear how the banjo and the harmony singing make the song stern and emotional at the same time?

artiest/the-staple-singers.text:
The Staple Singers was an American family group that sang gospel, soul and R&B. Roebuck Pops Staples, who moved from Mississippi to Chicago in the 1930s, formed the group with his children Cleotha, Pervis and Mavis. Yvonne later took Pervis's place. In 1948 they began singing in churches in Chicago, and in 1952 they signed their first contract. In those years the group sounded acoustic and gospel-folky, with Pops on guitar. At Vee-Jay Records they had hits with Uncloudy Day and Will the Circle Be Unbroken. Uncloudy Day made a deep impression on the young Bob Dylan.

In the 1960s Pops and his children were moved by the sermons of Martin Luther King and sang protest songs for civil rights, such as Freedom Highway. At Epic they sounded more pop in 1967 with Why (Am I Treated So Bad) and For What It's Worth. In 1968 came Stax Records, first with Steve Cropper and later with the producer Al Bell, in a funkier and more soulful direction. There came their big hits: Respect Yourself in 1971, I'll Take You There in 1972, which topped both Billboard charts, and If You're Ready (Come Go with Me) in 1973. After Stax went bankrupt, Curtis Mayfield made Let's Do It Again for them.

The group combined the message of the church with that of the civil rights movement and with the dance floor. In 1976 they sang in The Last Waltz by The Band, and in 1984 they reached the top of the dance chart with a cover of Slippery People by Talking Heads. In 1999 they were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Mavis Staples is still working as a solo artist.
artiest/the-staple-singers.listen: Listen to I'll Take You There and notice Mavis's high, warm voice above the loose groove, and the echo of the other voices. Can you hear the gospel roots beneath the soul?

artiest/the-stone-roses.text:
The Stone Roses were an English rock band from Manchester, formed in 1983. They were among the pioneers of the Madchester movement of the late 1980s and early 1990s. The best-known line-up consisted of the singer Ian Brown, the guitarist John Squire, the bassist Gary Mani Mounfield and the drummer Alan Reni Wren. Brown and Squire knew each other from school and at first tried out all sorts of little bands. Squire came up with the name Stone Roses as two words that contradict each other. Mani joined the group in late 1987, and according to Brown the sound changed almost overnight.

The debut album The Stone Roses appeared in 1989 on Silvertone and became a classic. Singles such as Made of Stone and She Bangs the Drums led to Fools Gold, which reached the top eight of the British chart in November 1989 and became the band's best-known song. The music combined 1960s-style guitar pop, with clear, jangling guitars and strong melodies, with the groove and dance of the time. A long legal battle with the label followed, until the group signed with Geffen in 1991. The second album, Second Coming, came in 1994 and received mixed reviews. After changes in the line-up the band stopped in 1996.

In 2011 the group got together again, with a world tour and three concerts at Heaton Park in Manchester, but after two singles in 2016 it was over again in 2017. The influence on British guitar music is great. The Gallagher brothers of Oasis named their performances as an inspiration.
artiest/the-stone-roses.listen: Listen to Fools Gold and notice the tight, repeating bass line and the guitar floating above it. Can you hear how this is a rock song that you can also dance to?

artiest/the-stooges.text:
The Stooges, also known as Iggy and the Stooges, were an American rock band from Ann Arbor, Michigan. The singer Iggy Pop founded the group in 1967 with the guitarist Ron Asheton, the drummer Scott Asheton and the bassist Dave Alexander. Pop was impressed by the Doors, and after a visit to Chicago he wanted to make a new kind of blues that did not lean on the past. The group began as the Psychedelic Stooges, and its first experiments were more avant-garde than punk, using household appliances such as a vacuum cleaner and a blender, feedback and home-made instruments.

In 1968 the band signed with Elektra, like the MC5. The first two records, The Stooges in 1969 and Fun House in 1970, sold poorly and received little praise at the time. The group was known, however, for wild, primitive performances, in which Pop smeared himself with peanut butter, cut himself with glass and dived into the audience. He is regarded as one of the inventors of stage diving. Then the band fell apart. With help from David Bowie, Raw Power appeared in 1973, with the guitarist James Williamson, a record that had its influence above all on early punks. In 1974 the group stopped. In 2003 the group returned, with The Weirdness in 2007 and Ready to Die in 2013 as the last records.

The Stooges are regarded as one of the most important proto-punk bands. The sound was raw, simple and menacing, and pointed ahead to the punk of the 1970s. In 2010 they were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/the-stooges.listen: Listen to I Wanna Be Your Dog from the debut album and notice the hammering, almost monotonous guitar riff and Iggy Pop's raw voice. Hear how little it takes to make a song sound menacing.

artiest/the-stranglers.text:
The Stranglers is an English rock band from Guildford in Surrey, formed in 1974. The classic line-up from 1975 to 1990 consisted of the guitarist and singer Hugh Cornwell, the bassist and singer Jean-Jacques Burnel, the keyboard player Dave Greenfield and the drummer Jet Black. Black had previously run a fleet of ice-cream vans and an off-licence, and used his money to form a band. The ice-cream vans served as the first tour buses. Cornwell was a blues musician, Burnel a classical guitarist, Black a jazz drummer, and Greenfield played on military bases in Germany. Their first influences were psychedelic rock bands such as The Doors.

The group first built up an audience in pub rock and from 1976 was linked with the emerging punk, partly through its support slots. Its aggressive attitude and grim lyrics fitted in with that, but the music remained idiosyncratic. The sound was carried by Burnel's heavy, melodic bass and by Greenfield's keyboards. Rattus Norvegicus and No More Heroes appeared in 1977, Black and White in 1978 and The Raven in 1979. La Folie in 1981 and Feline in 1982 followed, among others. Their biggest hit was Golden Brown in 1982, alongside Peaches, No More Heroes, Strange Little Girl and Skin Deep.

After Cornwell left in 1990 the line-up changed often. Black stopped in 2018 and Greenfield died in 2020, after which Burnel became the only original member still performing. The Stranglers are among the longest-surviving bands of the British punk scene. They showed that a punk band was also capable of refinement: from rude troublemakers to makers of fine pop songs, in the words of one critic.
artiest/the-stranglers.listen: Listen to No More Heroes by The Stranglers. Notice Burnel's heavy, melodic bass and how Greenfield's keyboard playing gives punk a colour of its own.

artiest/the-strokes.text:
The Strokes are an American rock band from New York, formed in 1998. The line-up has stayed the same since the beginning: the singer and main songwriter Julian Casablancas, the guitarists Nick Valensi and Albert Hammond Jr., the bassist Nikolai Fraiture and the drummer Fabrizio Moretti. Casablancas, Valensi and Moretti played together as teenagers at the Dwight School in Manhattan. Fraiture was a childhood friend of Casablancas. At the end of 1998 Hammond joined.

In 2001 the EP The Modern Age was released, which set off a bidding war between small labels. The group signed with RCA Records and released the debut album Is This It that year, with Last Nite. The album received praise from critics and has since appeared on many lists of the best albums. Room on Fire followed in 2003 and First Impressions of Earth in 2005. After a five-year break came Angles in 2011 and Comedown Machine in 2013. In 2020 The New Abnormal appeared, produced by Rick Rubin. That album won a Grammy for best rock album.

The Strokes were among the leaders of the garage rock revival and post-punk revival in the early 2000s. Their music is guitar-driven and tight, with interwoven guitar parts. They showed that rock with a simple line-up could sound fresh again.
artiest/the-strokes.listen: Listen to Last Nite and notice how the two guitars complement each other and how the drummer holds the tempo tightly throughout. Can you hear how the vocal sounds deliberately nonchalant?

artiest/the-style-council.text:
The Style Council was an English pop group that came into being in Woking at the end of 1982. Paul Weller started it shortly after the end of The Jam, together with the keyboard player Mick Talbot. He wanted to escape the straitjacket of the rock band and to explore pop, soul and hip hop. The group deliberately remained a loose association, with guest singers and later permanent members such as the drummer Steve White and the singer Dee C. Lee. In 1983 four separate singles followed that each sounded different: Speak Like a Child, Money-Go-Round, Long Hot Summer and A Solid Bond in Your Heart, all in the British top twenty. They appeared on the mini-album Introducing The Style Council.

In 1984 the debut album Café Bleu came out, with jazz, soul, pop and funk mixed together, which divided critics and confused fans. My Ever Changing Moods became a hit, in the United States too. With Our Favourite Shop in 1985 the group reached its peak in Britain. The album went straight to the top of the chart, with influences from Latin music, jazz and funk and mostly political lyrics, as in Walls Come Tumbling Down! and Come to Milton Keynes. That year the band played at Live Aid.

After that it went downhill. The Cost of Loving in 1987 opted for R&B and its successor Confessions of a Pop Group no longer reached the top ten. The album Modernism: A New Decade, with influences from house music, was something Polydor did not want to release, and it only appeared in 1998. In 1989 Weller and Talbot split up. The group also supported political causes, such as the Council Collective with the single Soul Deep for striking miners, and was active in Red Wedge.
artiest/the-style-council.listen: Listen to My Ever Changing Moods and notice the shifting mood between the driving piano and the vocal. Hear how a pop song lets itself be influenced by jazz and soul.

artiest/the-sugarcubes.text:
The Sugarcubes, in Icelandic Sykurmolarnir, was an Icelandic alternative rock band from Reykjavik. It was formed in 1986 and ceased to exist in 1992. The line-up consisted mainly of Björk Guðmundsdóttir (vocals, keyboards), Einar Örn Benediktsson (vocals, trumpet), Þór Eldon (guitar), Bragi Ólafsson (bass), Margrét Örnólfsdóttir (keyboards) and the drummer Sigtryggur Baldursson. The members came from other Icelandic bands. Björk had already recorded an album at the age of eleven and later sang in the post-punk band Tappi Tíkarrass. In 1984 she, Einar Örn and Sigtryggur formed the group Kukl, which released two albums on the British label Crass Records.

The Sugarcubes came into being on 8 June 1986. According to the band, the name probably did not refer to LSD, but to the idea of a cute pop band, in contrast with what the members had made before. At the end of 1987 they signed with One Little Indian in the United Kingdom and Elektra in the United States. The debut album Life's Too Good appeared in 1988 and was an unexpected international success. The BBC DJ John Peel played the song Birthday, which became a signature song of the group. In 1989 came Here Today, Tomorrow Next Week! and in 1992 Stick Around for Joy, with the singles Hit and Leash Called Love.

The music is called avant-pop, with a psychedelic post-punk sound that sometimes recalls the B-52's and Talking Heads. Striking are the whimsical lyrics, Björk's urgent, almost childlike voice and the rougher voice of Einar Örn that stands against it. The album is regarded as the first Icelandic album with worldwide influence. Rolling Stone called the group the greatest rock band from Iceland. After the Sugarcubes Björk began a solo career and became the best-selling Icelandic musician ever.
artiest/the-sugarcubes.listen: Listen to Birthday by The Sugarcubes. Notice the interplay between Björk's voice and Einar Örn's, and the strange, playful atmosphere of the song.
